title: 道德經 第四十八章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 48, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 76. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 48 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 忘知 (Forgetting Knowledge). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

morph.gloss: wéi: to do, to go in for, to pursue
learning, book-study — the piling up of distinctions
the sun, a day — here adverbially: by the day, daily
to increase, to add to; a gain

sentences.l: Doing learning, day by day gaining;
sentences.i: Pursue learning, and every day there is more.
sentences.n:
為 is wéi and takes an ordinary object: 為學 is doing-learning, going in for study. (The house default holds — 為 is wèi 'for the sake of' only where the complement is plainly benefactive, and 學 here is what is done, not what it is done for.)

日 is the noun 'day' used as an adverb, 'by the day', with nothing at all marking the shift. Classical Chinese does this constantly, and position is the only signal.

There is no subject and no tense. The line is not a report about somebody; it is a rule, and it waits for its opposite number in the next unit before it means anything. The Guodian bamboo slips of about 300 BC carry this opening, with small differences of wording — it is among the oldest material in the book.

morph.gloss: to diminish, to take from, to subtract; a loss

sentences.l: Doing the Way, day by day losing.
sentences.i: Pursue the Way, and every day there is less.
sentences.n:
The couplet is the whole argument: what learning piles up, the Way takes away. 益 and 損 are a standing pair in Chinese thought — increase and decrease, the two sides of a ledger, and the names of two of the Yijing's hexagrams.

The book is not against knowing things. It is saying that the Way is not another subject to be added to what one knows: it is reached by subtraction, and every chapter that praises the uncarved block or the newborn is saying this same thing in another figure.

sentences.t:
損之又損，
以至於無為。
無為而無不為。

morph.gloss: it — the object pronoun, not the genitive; what is taken from is left unsaid
at — the preposition after its verb
acting without forcing — doing that adds no contrivance and no strain against the grain of things; not idleness
wéi: done — 無不為, 'there is nothing not done'

sentences.l:
Take from it, and again take from it,
and so arrive at acting-without-forcing.
Acting without forcing, and yet nothing not done.
sentences.i: Take away, and take away again, until you come to acting without forcing; and acting without forcing, there is nothing that does not get done.
sentences.n:
之 is the object pronoun, 'it', the second of that character's two jobs — and what the 'it' is, the line does not say. What you have piled up, presumably; and then the piler.

無不為 is a double negative, and the whole force of the chapter sits in it. Not 'nothing happens' but 'there is nothing that is not done': the claim is about the outcome, not the effort. Notice that 無為 is one word here, the book's term of art, while 無不為 is three separate characters — 無 不 為 — which is why the literal keeps them apart.

Whether 無為而無不為 stood in the earliest text is argued. The Guodian slips carry the opening of this chapter, and what they have at this point is read differently by different editors; we are not in a position to settle it and do not pretend to. What is worth knowing is why it is worth arguing about: with the clause, a counsel of restraint is also a promise of results. The received text has it, and so does this one.

morph.gloss: to take, to take hold of — here of winning the empire
all under heaven — the whole inhabited world and everyone in it
always, as a rule — the book's word for what abides, here adverbial
by means of, by way of
business, affairs, matters needing to be handled

sentences.l: The taking of all under heaven is always by way of having no business;
sentences.i: All under heaven is always won by keeping no business afoot;
sentences.n:
無事 answers 無為 and is not the same phrase: 事 is business — the matters a ruler keeps generating, the projects, the campaigns, the reforms — so 無事 is having none of them going. Unlike 無為 it has not become a term of art, which is why it stays two words.

取天下 is political and quite plain: to take, to get hold of, all under heaven. This is advice to a ruler, and the chapter's subtraction turns out to have been aimed at him from the start.

常 is chapter 1's 常, the abiding; standing before a preposition like this it comes out as 'always, as a rule'.

morph.gloss: to reach — at the head of a clause, 'when it comes to, once'
his — the possessive makes a noun of what follows: 'his having business'

sentences.l: and when it comes to his having business,
sentences.n:
及 heads the reversing clause: 'once, when it comes to'. 其有事 is the same nominalising as 其出 in chapter 47 — a possessive in front of a verb phrase turns it into a thing, 'his having business', exactly as English does with 'his leaving'.

The literal keeps this unit unfinished because the Chinese does: the sense-unit stops mid-sentence, where Wang Bi's commentary breaks it, and the verb does not arrive until the next one.

morph.gloss: enough, sufficient — 不足以 X, 'not enough to X'
all under heaven — the whole inhabited world and everyone in it

sentences.l: he is not enough to take all under heaven.
sentences.i: he is not equal to the taking of all under heaven.
sentences.n:
不足以 X is the standing negative of capacity — 'not enough to X', 'not up to X-ing' — and it is worth learning as a unit, since it turns up wherever the book measures a man against a task.

The chapter closes by saying its own words backwards: 取天下 opened the sentence and now ends it, with the condition between them reversed. And 足 is the character chapter 46 built its ending on — enough. There, enough was what you knew you had; here, it is what the meddler is not.
